doc.title: Jon-Erik Kellso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Youth bands and the International Youth Symphony
summary: He played up through school, college and youth orchestras, and in seventh grade learned orchestral transposition in the International Youth Symphony.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Well you had a pretty good — I read a little bit about your school experience. You got in a youth orchestra, something like that?

Yeah, I started pretty quick. I mean early on I really took to playing the trumpet right away. I loved it and I just was one of those kids that my parents had to tell me to stop practicing, instead of trying to force me to practice. And so I progressed pretty rapidly. I practiced a lot and I played in — like when I was in elementary school I would sneak over and play with the junior high band, or they actually did ask me to come over to play with them to help out. And when I was in junior high I’d go and play with the high school band. When I was in high school I was playing with a college band.

Yeah, kind of. And I had good teachers who knew that that was a good thing for me, to push me as far as testing my limits and putting me in more challenging territory. And I guess it was seventh grade when a friend of mind, Mike Karoub, who is a cello player and bass player, his father was the junior high band director, where I grew up, and his father had gotten him into this group called the International Youth Symphony, which was basically, I was about the youngest guy in it. It was like junior high through college age, people mostly in the Detroit and Windsor areas. And so I started playing in seventh grade in this group, the International Youth Symphony, which was a good youth symphony, very good. And the conductor of the Windsor Symphony, Matti Holli was the conductor for that, and that was quite a challenge, because I hadn’t played any orchestral music yet at all, seventh grade you know. And all of a sudden they’re talking about transposing, reading A trumpet parts and C trumpet parts, and E flat trumpet parts, and I had never even heard of that yet. So I basically had to learn a lot real quick. And I did well. I always thrived on challenges like that.
I didn’t know that that was still required from trumpets — that they’d do that kind of thing.

Yeah. Orchestral, it’s standard. Actually the standard trumpet that they use in orchestras is a C trumpet, which is pitched differently than the standard band and jazz band trumpet which is in B flat. So yeah, almost everything was transposing. So it was a good experience.
